subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 20-year-old basketball player lands on an inverted foot and develops lateral ankle swelling, ecchymosis, and tenderness just below the lateral malleolus.
question: Which ligament is most commonly injured in this type of low ankle sprain?
explanation_correct: The anterior talofibular ligament is the most commonly injured ankle ligament overall and produces a low ankle sprain, typically from overinversion or supination of the foot. The anterior inferior tibiofibular ligament is the most common high ankle sprain. This patient's lateral tenderness after an inversion mechanism fits an ATFL injury.

explanation_incorrect.A: The posterior talofibular ligament is part of the lateral collateral complex but is less commonly injured than the anterior talofibular ligament.
explanation_incorrect.B: The calcaneofibular ligament can be injured in severe inversion sprains but is not the most common ligament injured.
explanation_incorrect.C: The anterior inferior tibiofibular ligament is the most common high ankle sprain, not a low ankle sprain.
explanation_incorrect.E: The posterior inferior tibiofibular ligament is part of the syndesmosis and is not the typical low sprain ligament.

educationalObjective: Identify the anterior talofibular ligament as the most common low ankle sprain.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A 25-year-old man sustains a forced external rotation injury with the ankle dorsiflexed. He has pain above the ankle and tenderness over the tibiofibular syndesmosis, with a widened tibiofibular clear space on radiographs.
question: Which ligament is most likely injured?
explanation_correct: The anterior inferior tibiofibular ligament is the most commonly injured ligament in high ankle sprains ('high tide'), typically from external rotation with dorsiflexion. It is part of the distal tibiofibular syndesmosis. This contrasts with the anterior talofibular ligament, the most common low ankle sprain caused by inversion.

explanation_incorrect.A: The anterior talofibular ligament is the most common low ankle sprain from overinversion, not a high ankle sprain.
explanation_incorrect.B: The calcaneofibular ligament is a lateral collateral ligament injured in inversion sprains.
explanation_incorrect.C: The posterior talofibular ligament is part of the lateral collateral complex, not the syndesmosis.
explanation_incorrect.D: The posterior inferior tibiofibular ligament is part of the syndesmosis but is not the most commonly injured high sprain ligament; the anterior inferior tibiofibular ligament is.

educationalObjective: Identify the anterior inferior tibiofibular ligament as the most common high ankle sprain.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: A surgeon dissecting the popliteal fossa identifies a nerve running alongside the popliteal artery. Naming conventions usually pair nerves and arteries by region, but several exceptions exist.
question: Which nerve accompanies the popliteal artery in the popliteal fossa?
explanation_correct: In the popliteal fossa, the tibial nerve accompanies the popliteal artery, one of the listed exceptions to neurovascular naming because there is no 'popliteal nerve.' The tibial nerve continues with the posterior tibial artery behind the medial malleolus. These pairings are high-yield anatomic relationships.

explanation_incorrect.A: The femoral nerve travels with the femoral artery in the femoral triangle, not in the popliteal fossa.
explanation_incorrect.B: The common peroneal nerve winds around the fibular neck and does not accompany the popliteal artery.
explanation_incorrect.C: The sciatic nerve divides in the distal thigh into tibial and common peroneal components.
explanation_incorrect.D: The obturator nerve enters the thigh through the obturator foramen with the obturator vessels.

educationalObjective: Recall that the tibial nerve pairs with the popliteal artery in the popliteal fossa.

subject: Musculoskeletal
vignette: During open reduction of a humeral shaft fracture, the surgeon identifies a nerve and artery traveling together in the radial groove on the posterior humerus.
question: Which neurovascular pair is being identified?

options.text: Axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery
Radial nerve and deep brachial artery
Long thoracic nerve and lateral thoracic artery

explanation_correct: At the midshaft of the humerus, the radial nerve travels with the deep brachial (profunda brachii) artery in the radial groove, a classic exception to neurovascular naming. Other exceptions include the axillary/posterior circumflex at the surgical neck, median/brachial in the cubital fossa, and long thoracic/lateral thoracic in the axilla. The radial groove location identifies this pair.

explanation_incorrect.A: The axillary nerve accompanies the posterior circumflex humeral artery at the surgical neck of the humerus, not the midshaft.
explanation_incorrect.B: The median nerve accompanies the brachial artery in the distal humerus/cubital fossa, not the radial groove.
explanation_incorrect.D: The long thoracic nerve and lateral thoracic artery are paired in the axilla and lateral thorax.
explanation_incorrect.E: The tibial nerve and popliteal artery are paired in the popliteal fossa, not the humerus.

educationalObjective: Recall that the radial nerve and deep brachial artery pair in the humeral radial groove.
